title: Service Boundaries Under Organizational Constraints
summary: Conway's Law means your org chart shows up in your architecture whether you plan for it or not, and platform-vs-product framing changes where a boundary should sit.

slides.markdown:
[service-decomposition](service-decomposition) covered drawing boundaries by business capability. This topic adds the layer senior engineers are expected to reason about: the org chart shapes the architecture regardless of whether anyone designs for it, so a "technically ideal" boundary that ignores team structure often fails in practice.

The skill here is choosing boundaries that are correct on both axes at once — domain-clean *and* aligned with who actually owns and operates each piece.

slides.sectionTitle: Conway's Law: systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them
slides.markdown:
Melvin Conway's 1968 observation, now called **Conway's Law**: "organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." In practice — if three teams barely talk to each other, the system they build will have roughly three loosely-coupled pieces, whether or not anyone planned it that way.

This isn't a metaphor; it's a mechanism. A developer on Team A who needs a change in Team B's code either waits on a cross-team request (slow, so they minimize how often they ask) or works around it (a workaround, a cached copy, a duplicated field) — and both responses shape the actual architecture over time, independent of any diagram.

The practical implication: you can't design a target architecture in isolation from the org that will build and run it — the two decisions are coupled whether you acknowledge it or not.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a boundary matching team ownership vs one cutting across three teams
slides.markdown:
![Aligned one-team-per-service vs three teams sharing one service](assets/conways-law-alignment.svg)

On the left, each team can change its own service without asking anyone; on the right, any change to the shared service requires syncing three teams' priorities and release schedules.

The right-hand shape is common when a service boundary was drawn for domain purity — "this is logically one bounded context" — without checking whether one team could realistically own it alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing boundaries for team autonomy, not just for domain purity
slides.markdown:
[service-decomposition](service-decomposition) taught drawing boundaries around bounded contexts. At expert level, add a second filter: **can exactly one team own this boundary end-to-end** — code, data, deploys, on-call — without needing another team's sign-off for routine changes?

Sometimes the domain-pure answer and the team-autonomy answer agree. When they don't — say, "Pricing" is logically one bounded context, but two teams (Promotions and Catalog) both need to own parts of it independently — the practical move is often to split along the *team* seam even if it means the domain model isn't textbook-clean, or to invest in reorganizing the teams to match the domain instead.

Either fix is legitimate. What's not viable long-term is a boundary that's domain-correct but has no single owning team — that setup reliably produces the coordination tax Conway's Law predicts.

slides.sectionTitle: Platform architecture vs product architecture: shared capability teams vs feature teams
slides.markdown:
Not every team should be structured the same way. **Stream-aligned (product) teams** own an end-to-end slice of user-facing functionality — Checkout, Search — and are measured on feature velocity for that slice. **Platform teams** own shared capabilities that many product teams depend on — auth, observability, the CI/CD pipeline, a shared data platform — and are measured on making other teams faster, not on shipping features themselves.

The architectural consequence: platform-owned services should be designed as **self-service** — a clean API or SDK a product team can adopt without a meeting — because the platform team can't scale linearly with the number of product teams asking for help. A platform team that requires a ticket and a two-week wait for every consumer request has effectively become a bottleneck team, defeating the point of separating platform from product.

Misdiagnosing which kind of team owns a service is a common expert-level mistake: treating a shared capability like a product feature (or vice versa) skews its whole API design.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: optimizing for Conway's Law alignment vs optimizing for the ideal domain model
slides.markdown:
| | Optimize for Conway's Law alignment | Optimize for the ideal domain model |
|---|---|---|
| Team velocity | High — each team owns its service without cross-team blocking | Can be low — a domain-pure boundary owned by no single team creates constant coordination |
| Domain cleanliness | Can be imperfect — boundaries may not match textbook bounded contexts | High — the model matches how a domain expert would describe the business |
| Risk if org changes | Boundaries can go stale as teams reorganize, needing periodic re-alignment | Stays valid longer, since it's independent of org structure |
| Best when | Team structure is stable and autonomy is the bottleneck | The org is small enough, or stable enough, that one team can own the whole clean model |

**How to decide:** in a growing org with several teams, weight team-alignment heavier — a slightly less pure domain model that one team owns cleanly beats a perfect model that needs three teams' agreement to change.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a technically clean service split that forces constant cross-team coordination
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We designed the ideal domain model and split services exactly along its bounded contexts — the architecture is correct."

**Why it's wrong:** correctness on paper doesn't survive contact with an org chart it ignores. If the "Pricing" service is domain-pure but two teams (Promotions, Catalog) both need to change it weekly, every release becomes a negotiation over whose change merges first — the team-coordination cost quietly becomes larger than the benefit of the clean model, and teams start routing around it with caches and workarounds anyway.

**Correct model:** treat "does exactly one team own this without needing another team's sign-off" as a first-class design constraint, equal in weight to domain purity — not an afterthought to fix once the coordination pain shows up in production.

slides.sectionTitle: The inverse Conway maneuver: restructuring teams to get the architecture you want
slides.markdown:
Conway's Law is usually stated descriptively (your system will mirror your org chart) but it has a prescriptive flip side: if you know the architecture you want, you can restructure the *teams* to produce it — the **inverse Conway maneuver**.

Concrete example: a company wants a clean separation between a checkout service and a fulfillment service, but currently has one team that owns both and constantly entangles them. Rather than trying to enforce a code-level boundary against the team's natural communication patterns, they split the team in two, each with its own on-call, backlog, and deploy pipeline — the codebase boundary that follows tends to hold much better than one imposed purely through documentation or code review, because now the org structure reinforces it instead of fighting it.

The takeaway: if a boundary keeps eroding despite repeated cleanup, the fix might be organizational, not technical — restructure the teams first and let the architecture follow, rather than re-drawing the same line in code for the third time.

slides.sectionTitle: Concrete symptoms that a boundary is wrong
slides.markdown:
A boundary that looks clean in a diagram can still be wrong in practice, and the tell is usually visible in day-to-day team friction before it shows up as a technical metric: a spike in cross-team pull requests needed to ship a single feature, two teams' on-call getting paged for the same incident because a "boundary" crosses their actual failure domain, or a feature that routinely needs sign-off from three different teams' roadmaps before it can ship.

If cross-team coordination for a single feature regularly needs sign-off from more than two teams, that's usually a sign the boundary was drawn around a domain concept rather than around who actually needs to move independently — the fix is to redraw the line around team ownership, even if it makes the domain model slightly less "clean" on paper.

**Testing:** whether you can name the concrete symptom (PR count, page-sharing, cross-team sign-off) that reveals a boundary is wrong, rather than only recognizing it in the abstract.
